lesson.title: Consistency First: Why Reliability Has to Come Before Validity
lesson.summary: Reliability is the consistency of a measurement across time, items, or raters, and it is a necessary but not sufficient condition for a test to be valid.
lesson.body:
Reliability refers to the consistency of a measurement: if you gave the same test to the same person under the same conditions multiple times, would you get roughly the same result each time? A classic, low tech way to picture this is a bathroom scale. If you step on a scale three times in a row and it reads 150 pounds, 162 pounds, and 141 pounds, the scale is unreliable, and it does not matter whether 150 happens to be your true weight, because you cannot trust any single reading to be dependable.

Psychologists assess reliability in several standard ways. Test retest reliability involves giving the same test to the same people at two different points in time and checking how strongly the two sets of scores correlate. Split half reliability divides a single test into two halves, often odd numbered and even numbered items, and checks whether people's scores on one half correlate with their scores on the other half, which gets at whether the test is measuring something consistently within itself. Internal consistency, often summarized with a statistic called Cronbach's alpha, extends this logic across all the items on a test at once. Inter rater reliability applies when scoring involves human judgment, such as grading an essay or coding a behavioral observation, and checks whether different raters arrive at similar scores for the same performance.

The relationship between reliability and validity, introduced in the previous chapter, is one of the more important ideas in this area, and it runs in only one direction. A test can be highly reliable without being valid at all. Returning to the bathroom scale: imagine a scale that is broken in a way that consistently reads exactly ten pounds heavier than your true weight every single time. That scale is now perfectly reliable, since it gives the same, consistent answer over and over, but it is not valid, since it systematically fails to measure your actual weight. What is not possible is the reverse: a test cannot be valid without also being reliable, because if a measurement bounces around unpredictably from one administration to the next, it cannot be dependably capturing the true underlying trait it claims to assess.

This is why reliability is often described as a necessary but not sufficient condition for validity. Test developers typically establish that a new measure is reliable first, since this is a comparatively straightforward statistical property to check, before undertaking the more difficult and time consuming work of building a full case for its validity. Both properties matter enormously for standardized testing, since a test that lacks either consistency or accuracy cannot be trusted to support the real decisions, from clinical diagnoses to school placements to job selection, that test scores are so often used to make.
